stages.title: Intermediate vocabulary
explain: Some French words look like English words but mean something different. They are called faux amis (false friends). "Une librairie" is a bookshop, not a library (that is "une bibliothèque"). "Actuellement" means at the moment, not actually.
Many words are true cousins: "la nation", "le restaurant", "important". Learn word families too: "travailler" (to work), "le travail" (work), "le travailleur" (worker).
sentences: I buy a book at the bookshop.
He is working at the moment.
We borrow books at the library.

gq.why: It is a false friend of English library.

panel.q: Why are false friends dangerous?
o: They look familiar so the meaning is assumed wrongly
panel.why: Similar form does not guarantee similar meaning.

panel.q: Which word is a true cognate of English "important"?
panel.why: Important has the same meaning in both languages.

panel.q: A learner says "Je vais assister la fête" to mean "I am going to attend the party". What is the problem?
o: Assister à means to attend; assister without à means to help
panel.why: The preposition changes the meaning.

teach.model: False friends look like English words but have another meaning, like librairie for bookshop. Word families link words, like travailler, le travail and le travailleur. Check unknown words in a dictionary.

stages.hook: The word "librairie" looks like "library", but is it? What other French words can trick an English speaker?
stages.mnemonic: Librairie sells books; bibliothèque lends them.

stages.title: Verb forms and time expressions
explain: The passé composé is the usual past tense for completed actions. It uses avoir or être plus a past participle: "J'ai mangé", "Elle est partie". Verbs of movement and reflexive verbs use être, and the participle agrees with the subject: "Elle est partie", "Ils sont partis".

The futur simple adds endings to the infinitive: "je mangerai", "tu mangeras", "il mangera". For the near future, use aller: "je vais manger". Time words help: hier (yesterday), aujourd'hui (today), demain (tomorrow), déjà (already), bientôt (soon).

gq.q: Choose the correct form: Hier, nous ___ au cinéma.
gq.why: Aller takes être in the passé composé.

gq.q: Why is it "Elle est partie" with an e?
o: The participle agrees with the subject when être is used
gq.why: With être, the past participle agrees with the subject.

panel.q: What is the futur simple of "parler" for tu?
panel.why: Future endings are added to the infinitive.

panel.q: Which sentence shows the near future?
panel.why: Aller plus the infinitive expresses the near future.

panel.q: Why does "J'ai mangé" not change for a woman speaking?
o: With avoir the participle stays unchanged here
panel.why: Agreement with avoir only happens with a direct object before the verb.

points.ask: How do I form the past?
How do I say the future?

teach.model: For completed past actions use the passé composé: avoir or être plus a participle. Verbs of movement use être and the participle agrees. For the future add endings to the infinitive or use aller plus an infinitive.

stages.hook: How do you say "I ate yesterday" and "I will eat tomorrow" in French?

stages.title: Complex sentence introduction
explain: Use conjunctions: "et" (and), "mais" (but), "ou" (or), "parce que" (because), "quand" (when), "si" (if), "pour que" (so that). Example: "Je reste à la maison parce qu'il pleut."

Relative pronouns link a noun to more information. "Qui" replaces the subject: "Le garçon qui joue est mon frère." "Que" replaces the object: "Le livre que je lis est intéressant." Before a vowel, que and si lose their vowel in "qu'il" and "s'il".
sentences: I stay at home because it is raining.
The book that I read is good.
If it rains, we stay here.

gq.q: Choose the correct word: La fille ___ chante est ma sœur.
gq.why: Qui is the subject of chante.

gq.q: Why is it "s'il pleut" and not "si il pleut"?
o: Si drops its vowel before il
gq.why: Si elides only before il and ils.

panel.q: Which is correct?
o: Le film que j'ai vu est drôle.
Le film qui j'ai vu est drôle.
Le film où j'ai vu est drôle.
Le film dont j'ai vu est drôle.
panel.why: Que replaces the object (j'ai vu le film).

panel.q: What does "bien que" express?
panel.why: It introduces a contrast and takes the subjunctive.

panel.q: Why does "parce que" become "parce qu'" before a vowel?
o: Que elides before a vowel sound
panel.why: Elision applies to que.

teach.model: Conjunctions like et, mais, parce que and quand join ideas. Qui replaces the subject and que replaces the object. Que and si drop their vowel before a vowel sound, like qu'il and s'il.

stages.hook: How do you join two ideas, such as "I stay home because it is raining"?
stages.mnemonic: Qui is the doer, que is the receiver.

stages.title: Reading short stories
explain: French fables like those of Jean de La Fontaine teach morals with animals. In "Le Renard et les Raisins", a fox cannot reach grapes, so it says they are too green. The words "ils sont trop verts" have become a saying for pretending you do not want what you cannot have.

Stories often use the passé simple in writing (il dit, elle partit) and the imparfait for the setting (il faisait beau). In speech, the passé composé replaces the passé simple. Reading skills: find who, where, when, and what happens.
sentences: Once upon a time there was a king.
Suddenly the fox sees the grapes.

gq.q: Which writer is famous for French fables?
gq.why: La Fontaine wrote fables in the seventeenth century.

gq.q: Why is the imparfait used in "Il faisait beau"?
gq.why: The imparfait sets scenes and continuing states.

panel.q: What does "ils sont trop verts" mean as a saying?
o: Pretending you do not want what you cannot get
panel.why: It is a metaphor for sour grapes.

panel.q: Why does a story often start with "Il était une fois"?
o: It is the standard tale opening
panel.why: It signals a story and uses the imparfait.

panel.q: Why is the passé simple rarely spoken today?
o: It is mainly a literary tense
panel.why: Spoken French uses the passé composé.

teach.model: In a French tale, find who, where, when and what happens. The imparfait describes the scene and the passé composé or passé simple tells events. Fables like La Fontaine's end with a moral.

stages.hook: Read this short tale: a fox sees grapes but cannot reach them. What does it say?
stages.mnemonic: Imparfait paints the scene; passé composé moves the plot.

stages.title: Listening comprehension
explain: When listening, do not translate every word. Catch the key words: numbers, names, places and time words. Predict from context: at a station you expect times, platforms and tickets.

Pay attention to liaison and elision: "un_ami", "j'ai" and "l'ami" run together. Learn common spoken reductions: "t'es" for "tu es", "j'sais pas" for "je ne sais pas". Repeat audio at slower speed, then at normal speed.
sentences: The train leaves at eight o'clock.
Platform two is on the left.

gq.q: What is a good listening strategy?
o: Catch key words and use context
Stop listening if you miss a word
gq.why: Key words and context let you follow the meaning.

gq.q: "T'es là?" is a spoken reduction of:
gq.why: In speech tu es often becomes t'es.

panel.q: At a station you hear "Le train de Lyon est en retard". What does it say?
o: The train to Lyon is late
panel.why: En retard means late.

panel.q: Why does "les amis" sound like "lez ami"?
o: Liaison links a silent s to a vowel
panel.why: A normally silent consonant is said before a vowel.

panel.q: Why can two listeners understand the same announcement differently?
panel.why: Prediction from context affects comprehension.

teach.model: Listen for key words like numbers and places. Use context to guess. Notice liaison, elision and spoken reductions like t'es. Ask for repetition if needed.

stages.hook: You hear "Il est huit heures et demie." What helps you understand a fast spoken sentence?
stages.mnemonic: Hear the key words, guess the rest.

stages.title: Conversation and pronunciation
explain: The French r is made at the back of the throat. The vowel u (as in "tu") is said with rounded lips and the tongue as for "i". The nasal vowels are an, on, in and un. French syllables have almost equal stress; only the last syllable of a group is slightly longer.
Practise minimal pairs: "tu" and "tout", "pain" and "pont", "rue" and "roue". Use fillers such as "alors", "bon", "euh" and "ben" to keep speech natural.
sentences: The bread is on the table.

gq.q: How is the French u in "tu" made?
o: With rounded lips and the tongue as for i
gq.why: French u is a front rounded vowel.

gq.q: Why are "rue" and "roue" a useful pair?
o: They differ only by the vowel u or ou
gq.why: They train the difference between /y/ and /u/.

panel.q: Which word has a nasal vowel?
panel.why: In pont the o is nasal.

panel.q: Where is the stress in French?
o: At the end of a rhythm group
On the first syllable of each word
panel.why: French has fixed stress on the last syllable of a group.

panel.q: Why does an English accent make "tu" sound like "tout"?
o: English lacks the rounded front vowel u
panel.why: Learners replace /y/ with /u/.

teach.model: The French u is said with rounded lips and the tongue for i. The r is made in the throat. Nasal vowels are said through the nose. French stress falls at the end of a group. Practise minimal pairs like rue and roue.

stages.hook: How can you sound natural when speaking French? Which sounds are hardest?
stages.mnemonic: Round your lips for u: tu, rue, dur.

stages.title: Writing paragraphs
explain: A paragraph has an opening sentence, support, and a closing sentence. Use linking words: "d'abord" (first), "ensuite" (then), "puis" (next), "enfin" (finally), "par exemple" (for example), "cependant" (however).
Check your writing for agreement, accents and verb endings. Example: "D'abord, je me lève à sept heures. Ensuite, je mange du pain. Enfin, je vais à l'école."
sentences: First I get up at seven.

gq.q: Why are linking words useful in a paragraph?
gq.why: Connectors show order, contrast or cause.

panel.q: Which connector shows contrast?
panel.why: Cependant means however.

panel.q: Which connector shows a result?
panel.why: Donc means therefore.

panel.q: What is a good checking routine after writing?
o: Check agreement, accents, verb endings and spelling
panel.why: These are the typical sources of French errors.

teach.model: Begin with an opening sentence, then give support and end with a closing sentence. Use d'abord, ensuite, puis and enfin to order ideas, and cependant for contrast. Check agreement and accents.

stages.hook: How do you write a short paragraph in French that sounds connected?
stages.mnemonic: D'abord, ensuite, enfin: first, next, last.

stages.title: Cultural expressions and idioms
explain: Idioms mean something different from their words. "Il pleut des cordes" means it is raining heavily. "Avoir le cafard" means to feel low. "Poser un lapin" means to stand someone up. "Coûter les yeux de la tête" means to cost a fortune.

Cultural expressions include "Bon appétit" before eating, and "Santé!" when raising a glass. In France, people often greet each other with "la bise" (kisses on the cheek), but customs vary by region and relationship.
items: coûter les yeux de la tête

gq.q: What does "Il pleut des cordes" mean?
o: There are ropes in the sky
gq.why: It is an idiom for heavy rain.

gq.q: Why is it a mistake to translate "poser un lapin" word for word?
o: It means to stand someone up, not to put a rabbit
It means to leave a pet
gq.why: Idioms have fixed meanings that are not the sum of the words.

panel.q: What do you say before a meal?
panel.why: Bon appétit is said before eating.

panel.q: What does "la bise" depend on?
panel.why: The number of kisses varies by region and situation.

panel.q: Why do idioms help understanding of a culture?
o: They reflect shared images and experiences
panel.why: Idioms carry cultural history and humour.

points.ask: What does il pleut des cordes mean?
What do I say at meals?

teach.model: An idiom has a fixed meaning that differs from its words, like il pleut des cordes for heavy rain. Learn idioms as whole phrases. Say Bon appétit before a meal and Santé when you drink.

stages.hook: If someone says "Il pleut des cordes", is it raining ropes?
stages.mnemonic: Do not translate idioms word for word; learn them as pictures.

stages.title: Practical travel communication
explain: Useful phrases: "Où est la station de métro?", "Un billet, s'il vous plaît", "À quelle heure part le train?" and "Je cherche l'hôtel." For directions: tout droit (straight on), à gauche (left), à droite (right).

At a restaurant ask "L'addition, s'il vous plaît." At a hotel say "J'ai une réservation." In an emergency say "Au secours!" and "J'ai besoin d'aide." Politeness is key: begin with "Excusez-moi" or "Bonjour".
sentences: Excuse me, where is the station?
Turn left, then go straight on.

gq.q: You want directions. What do you say first?
Why is "vous" used with a stranger?

panel.q: What does "tout droit" mean?
panel.why: Tout droit is straight ahead.

panel.q: Which phrase would you use in an emergency?
panel.why: Au secours means help.

panel.q: Why start a request with "Bonjour"?
o: In French culture greeting first is expected
panel.why: Skipping the greeting can seem impolite.

points.ask: How do I ask for help?

teach.model: Be polite: start with Bonjour or Excusez-moi, use vous and say s'il vous plaît. Ask directions with Où est? and understand tout droit, à gauche and à droite. In an emergency say Au secours.

stages.hook: You arrive in Paris and need a metro ticket. What do you say?
stages.mnemonic: Excusez-moi opens doors; merci closes them.
